description: Calling all space enthusiasts and curious explorers! 🚀 We're Lunar Mavericks, building Lunar Outpost: Mission NOVA. It is a a fun astronaut simulated training  environments where kids can tackle real challenges using NASA data. Come join us! No need to be an expert—just bring your curiosity, ideas, and excitement to build something awesome together!
summary:
Team Lunar Mavericks has developed an interactive game that serves as an initial training ground for young aspiring astronauts in the age group of 7-14 years old. Set in a lunar outpost, the game allows players to manage simulated scenarios inspired by real-life challenges faced during past space missions.

 The challenge asks us to design and build an interactive game or app that lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost, where they will learn to face real-life-like situations. In the game we developed, users take a mission-driven approach to balancing competing demands on critical resources. The tackling of these challenges, teach key decision-making principles that help them think critically, evaluate trade-offs, and navigate uncertainty.

We are increasingly becoming a spacefaring civilization. We will be setting up bases on the Moon and eventually Mars. To become contributing citizens we need to be trained in areas more than science and technology.  Critical thinking, sound decision-making, and the ability to navigate ambiguity will be equally important Developing these skills early will help prepare the next generation for a future that is quickly becoming a reality, while keeping alive the excitement and sense of wonder that the final frontier inspires

Project Details – Lunar Outpost: Mission NOVA

https://github.com/spaceanary/lunar-outpost-mission-nova

Presentation: https://github.com/spaceanary/lunar-outpost-mission-nova/blob/main/public/Lunar_Mavericks_Mission_NOVA_FINAL.pptx

Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Buk9YdDP_6I

Team: Lunar Mavericks

1. Our Idea: Learning to Think Like an Astronaut

Space exploration is exciting, but it is also incredibly challenging. Humans need to be trained in many different ways, and experiencing different challenges under varying constraints can be far more impactful than simply learning through books or watching online content. Facing these challenges in real life can be extremely costly, but what if we could use the wealth of data collected over the past decades to recreate real-life scenarios in a simulated environment? This would allow us to experience similar situations, make decisions, learn from mistakes, and gain valuable lessons without the risks and costs of real-world experimentation.

We wanted to recreate some of these past situations by adapting them for children in a way that was fun, interactive, educational, and easy to understand. In our game, children become junior astronauts who are responsible for helping operate a lunar outpost. They encounter realistic space-related challenges, learn the science behind them, and make decisions that affect their mission.

Our goal was not to create a space quiz or a game where children collect points or are dinged for bad decisions or incorporate heavy jargon.  We wanted to create an environment where children could experience what it is to think critically, understand consequences, and develop the confidence to make decisions because, sometimes there is obvious or perfect answer.

Our project is a simulation-based game meant to train young kids in problems they could be facing when deployed into deep space as future astronauts. When the user first opens the game, they are introduced to the NOVA, the mission assistant, an AI voice that helps guide the player on their commanding journey. They are assigned the role of commander, and told about their responsibilities on managing the team. The player is then presented with six different space weather patterns, and are able to learn about them individually. For purposes of keeping young audiences engaged, each weather pattern has its own name. Next, they are prompted to choose one of three missions. As soon as the mission starts, the user is provided with three pieces of “evidence” which is specific to the mission. Once they have read all the pieces of evidence, they are able to start the mission.

2. How the Game Works

The game takes place at a fictional lunar outpost. They are oriented to different parts of the base, including the habitat, solar power systems, radiation shielding, food production, and communications.

Players can explore the outpost and select missions based on their interests. Each mission focuses on a different challenge inspired by real space science and engineering. Players receive mission information, examine the available options, make decisions, and observe what happens next.

Sometimes a choice improves one part of the mission while creating a problem somewhere else. This is intentional.

We wanted children to understand that real-world problems are rarely solved by finding one perfect answer. Good decisions often require balancing several competing priorities.

Game Mechanics:

  • Intro in game to give user background on the game and help them understand how the game works
  • Trains young kids in deep space decision making
  • The user plays the game as a commander managing their mission’s fate
  • They are prompted, in three separate missions, to make choices based on   weather patterns that affect lunar base
  • Before each mission starts, “evidence” is provided to help the user learn about the potential setbacks that the weather pattern could create
  • Each mission starts with a simulation 
  • Then, based on what the user decides (clicks multiple choice), a result stems from it
  • They are then told to manage that result
  • The user cannot lose; if they chose the wrong option, NOVA guides them to make better decision

 

Mission 01: Space Weather and Crew Safety

Objective: Our first mission introduces children to the dangers of space weather and the importance of protecting astronauts from radiation. To make this science easier to understand, we introduced friendly characters representing different space weather phenomena:

  • Flicker represents solar flares.
  • Bloop represents coronal mass ejections (CMEs).
  • Zip & Zap represent solar energetic particles.

How: Each character helps explain a different scientific concept in a memorable and approachable way.

As the mission progresses, players must interpret space weather information, evaluate potential risks, and decide how to protect their crew.

Data Inspiration: We incorporated historical information from NASA's DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information) to connect the learning experience with actual recorded space weather events.

We made a conscious effort to distinguish real NASA scientific information from fictional mission scenarios and illustrative gameplay values.

Purpose: The purpose of this mission is not simply to teach children what a solar flare is. It is to help them understand how scientific information can support real decisions.

Mission 02: Power Under Pressure – Every Watt Counts

Objective: Our second mission explores one of the most important challenges of living on the Moon: managing limited resources. In this mission, players must manage the outpost's resources while responding to changing conditions and an emergency involving the habitat's life-support systems. They face decisions such as whether to prioritize essential systems, conserve energy, or temporarily reduce power to less critical activities.

 

How: In this mission, players must manage the outpost's resources while responding to changing conditions and an emergency involving the habitat's life-support systems. They face decisions such as whether to prioritize essential systems, conserve energy, or temporarily reduce power to less critical activities. The challenge becomes more interesting because resources are interconnected.

For example, conserving power may help the outpost remain operational longer, but reducing power to the wrong system could compromise crew safety.

Data Inspiration: The inspiration came from the resource constraints and engineering challenges faced during real space missions, including Apollo and Artemis, as well as the experience of NASA's Opportunity rover during the 2018 Martian dust storm. Although Opportunity was a robotic mission on Mars rather than a crewed lunar mission, its experience provides a powerful example of how environmental conditions and limited energy can affect mission survival.

Purpose: A lunar outpost cannot assume that power, oxygen, and other essential resources will always be available in unlimited quantities. Through this mission, children practice prioritization, systems thinking, resource management, and understanding trade-offs. Most importantly, they learn that solving one problem should not create a bigger problem somewhere else.

Mission 03: Communication and Mission Autonomy

Objective: Our third mission focuses on another critical part of space exploration: communication. Astronauts depend on communication systems to exchange information with Earth, coordinate activities, and receive mission support. In Mission 03, players face communication-related challenges and must decide how to keep their lunar outpost operating safely.

How: The mission introduces ideas such as communication reliability, prioritizing important messages, and deciding when a crew should act independently rather than wait for instructions.

We wanted this mission to teach something especially relevant beyond space exploration.

Purpose: In real life, children will not always have someone available to tell them exactly what to do. They need to learn how to evaluate situations, identify what matters most, and make thoughtful decisions using the information they have.

3. The Learning Philosophy Behind Mission NOVA

One of the most important parts of our project is the thinking process we want children to develop. We believe children should learn not only scientific facts but also how to apply those facts when solving problems. Throughout the game, we introduce decision-making principles that are useful both in space and in everyday life.

These include:

Thinking in probabilities rather than certainties: Understanding that decisions often involve uncertainty and that we may not know exactly what will happen.

Recognizing reversible and irreversible decisions: Learning that some choices can be changed easily, while others require greater caution.

Testing working hypotheses: Considering possible explanations and using evidence rather than jumping to conclusions.

Systems thinking: Understanding how different resources and systems depend on one another.

Opportunity cost and prioritization: Recognizing that choosing one action may mean giving up another.

Feedback and adaptability: Observing what happens after a decision and adjusting when new information becomes available.

Navigating Uncertainty  : Learning that waiting for perfect information is not always possible.

Rather than teaching these ideas as a separate classroom lesson, we wanted children to experience them through the missions. Our hope is that children gradually begin applying these principles without even realizing they are learning them.

4. How We Used NASA Data and Real Space Missions

We wanted our game to be imaginative, but we also wanted it to have a strong scientific foundation. We used these resources to help shape our missions.

One of the most important resources for our project was NASA DONKI, which provides information about recorded space weather events, including solar flares, coronal mass ejections, and solar energetic particle events. We also drew inspiration from real engineering challenges encountered during NASA missions. The Apollo missions demonstrated the importance of managing limited spacecraft resources and responding to unexpected problems. The Artemis program provides a modern context for the challenges involved in returning humans to the Moon and supporting future lunar exploration.

NASA's Opportunity rover provided another valuable lesson. During a major dust storm on Mars in 2018, sunlight reaching the rover's solar panels was dramatically reduced, affecting its ability to generate power.

These examples helped us design missions around meaningful scientific and engineering challenges rather than arbitrary obstacles.

Our game uses real scientific concepts and historical inspiration, while the lunar outpost, characters, decisions, and some resource values are simplified for educational gameplay.

Inspiration for energy resilience and contingency planning. Opportunity's solar-powered operations were disrupted by a severe Martian dust storm in June 2018. This historical event inspires general power-management lessons; the fictional lunar scenario does not recreate Martian weather.

NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR)
https://osdr.nasa.gov/bio/repo/

Additional educational research resource for space biology and potential future mission development. OSDR research data is not directly integrated into the current gameplay.

 

5. Technology and Tools We Used

We developed Lunar Outpost: Mission NOVA as a web-based application so that children can access it through a browser without installing special software.

Our main development tools and technologies include:

  • React: Used to build the interactive game interface, mission screens, and reusable components.
  • TypeScript: Used to implement gameplay logic, mission states, resource management, and player interactions.
  • JavaScript: Used as part of the web application's underlying functionality.
  • HTML and CSS: Used to create the game's layout, visual design, responsive elements, animations, and interface styling.
  • Vite: Used for the frontend development and build process.
  • StackBlitz: Used as our browser-based development environment, allowing us to build and test the application quickly.
  • GitHub: Used for source-code management and tracking changes.
  • Netlify: Used to deploy the application and make it accessible online.
  • NASA Open APIs and DONKI resources: Used to bring real scientific information into the educational experience.
  • Elevenlabs for voice intro of Nova

We also used  AI-assisted development tools like Chatgpt and Claude to help with prototyping, brainstorming ( what if scenarios etc.) coding, debugging, and refining the experience.

The application does not require specialized hardware lightweight web-based approach because accessibility was an important consideration for us so that a student could open at home or in a classroom without complicated setup requirements.

6. What Makes Our Project Creative?

We believe the creativity of Mission NOVA comes from combining scientific learning, storytelling, and decision-making into one experience. While, many educational games focus on remembering facts or selecting the correct answer from a list – we wanted to have learning happen through  the consequences of a child's decisions?

·       Instead of asking children to memorize the definition of a solar flare, we place them in a situation where understanding a solar flare helps them protect their crew.

·       Instead of explaining why energy conservation matters, we give them a limited power budget and let them experience the trade-offs involved.

·       Instead of simply describing communication delays, we challenge them to make decisions when communication becomes unreliable.

We wanted the game to feel welcoming and inspiring, capturing the excitement and urgency of a high-stakes space mission without overwhelming or intimidating young players.

NOVA serves as a guide who helps players understand what is happening without taking away their responsibility for making decisions.

Another design choice was to allow players to access missions independently. Each mission can serve as its own learning experience while contributing to the larger theme of lunar exploration.

7. Important Factors We Considered During Development

While developing Mission NOVA, we had to make several design decisions.

Making the science understandable without making it inaccurate

Our target audience is young, but we did not want to underestimate their ability to understand complex ideas. We tried to explain scientific concepts in simple language while preserving the important distinctions. For example, solar flares, CMEs, and solar energetic particles are related to space weather, but they are not the same phenomenon. We wanted children to understand these differences rather than treat all space weather events as interchangeable.

Giving decisions meaningful consequences

We wanted choices to matter.

In a real mission, decisions often involve trade-offs. Protecting one resource may place pressure on another. Our resource indicators and mission outcomes were designed to help players see those relationships. We also wanted children to understand why a decision succeeded or failed rather than simply receiving a score.

Encouraging learning from mistakes

We did not want children to feel that making a wrong decision meant they had failed. In engineering and science, mistakes can provide valuable information. Our approach encourages children to reflect on the consequences of their decisions and consider how they might respond differently.

Keeping the experience accessible

We considered the limited attention span of younger players, the importance of clear navigation, and the need to avoid overwhelming them with information. This influenced our interface design, use of visual indicators, mission structure, and the way NOVA introduces information.

Building something that can grow

Although we developed the initial experience for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we wanted the concept to have potential beyond the competition. That influenced our decision to use a modular, mission-based structure rather than building one long, fixed storyline.

8. Future Possibilities

We see the current version of Mission NOVA as the beginning of a larger educational idea. The lunar outpost gives us a foundation for introducing many additional challenges.

Future missions could explore growing food in space, managing water supplies, repairing damaged equipment, navigating lunar terrain, responding to medical emergencies, or designing more sustainable lunar habitats.

We could also imagine a classroom mode where students work together, discuss possible solutions, and compare their reasoning.

Over time, Mission NOVA could evolve into a collection of interactive STEM learning experiences covering the Moon, Mars, and other areas of space exploration.

Our long-term vision is to make scientific thinking more accessible through experiences that encourage curiosity, experimentation, and thoughtful decision-making.

10. What We Hope Children Take Away

If there is one thing we hope children remember after playing Mission NOVA, it is that being an astronaut is not just about knowing a lot about space.

A child who learns to manage limited power on the Moon is also learning about prioritization. A child who responds to a solar storm is learning to assess risks. A child who navigates a communication failure is learning to make decisions independently.

That is the idea behind Lunar Outpost: Mission NOVA.

Because the next generation of explorers needs more than answers. They need to know how to think.
